name: South Slope and Ridge
approach: There is no trailhead in the usual sense — you step off the highway into the forest. Drive SR 20 to the bridge over Gorge Creek, about 2.6 miles east of Newhalem near milepost 122, or about the same distance west of the Gorge Lake causeway and the Diablo turnoff. Watch the sharp turn at the east end of the bridge. There are parking lots at each end; the east lot is signed for motorhomes and oversize vehicles, so park at the west lot. Elevation here is 1,096 ft, and there are accessible restrooms and a short interpretive trail to the Gorge Creek Falls viewpoint. From the east lot, walk a few feet east, cross the highway, and pick the easiest place to start uphill into the woods. That is the whole approach: the route and the approach are the same thing from here, 6,000 vertical feet of it. Round trip is about 6.2 miles with roughly 6,000 ft of gain in three miles. Carry water. The slope is south-facing and dry once the snow is gone, and there is no reliable source between the highway and the snowfields high on the mountain. In late spring, snowmelt on the route solves this and simultaneously suppresses the brush, which is why that window is the usual recommendation.
descent_text:
Descend the south ridge crest directly rather than reversing the east-basin variation. The step that drops into the saddle looks formidably steep from camp — steep enough that at least one party detoured around it on the way up — but it is climbed down easily, with all the ledges you need. Below the saddle, retrace your line through Point 5872 and the open slopes.

The work is in the forest. Stay on the line you came up: the cliff bands near 2,400 ft and 2,800 ft need to be turned on the correct side, and getting them wrong means rappelling off trees. Slabs low on the mountain are covered in slippery moss, and one party reported a 3rd-class chimney with an awkward move below it as the crux of the descent. Expect deadfall fields. Total descent time is about 4.1 hours from the summit for a fit party moving well, and every account calls it brutal on the knees.

If you are descending this route after climbing the northeast face, the strong advice from the party that did it is to get the top 1,500 ft done in daylight — that is what lets you avoid the cliff bands — and to carry a compass, because the timber is dense enough to hide the dam lights and a drift to the north puts you back in Stetattle Creek.
beta:
Almost all the difficulty here is brush, steepness and route-finding rather than climbing. The rock is rated Class 4, but that grade comes from a climber who climbed it in January and has been honest about the limits of that experience — he can only guess at the difficulty of the rock and the number of pitches, if any, because good snow may have covered the harder steps.

From the Gorge Creek bridge at 1,096 ft the slope is sustained from the first step, gaining roughly 1,800 ft in the first half mile through small evergreens with a salal and brush understory. There is no trail, and numerous rock outcrops make navigation important. One recorded line: from near the highway curve, hike due north to about 2,800 ft, turn northeast and ascend to the 4,920+ ft point, then go straight uphill on a bearing of about 340 degrees true to Point 5872, where the south ridge becomes obvious. A party approaching via Gorge Creek instead took the South Buttress, turning cliff bands at about 2,400 ft and 2,800 ft on the right, moving through open timber and alpine snowfields, and reaching the South Davis saddle at 5,700 ft in 4.4 hours from the car; they described Class 2-3 scrambling on the buttress with slime-coated rock slabs near the top. A third account has the granite slabs starting around 4,850 ft after a brushy gully at 3,600 ft, bypassing Point 5872 to the north, and reaching a south-ridge viewpoint at 6,300 ft.

From the 5,720+ ft saddle, climb 200 ft of slab to the sharp ridge that leads to the summit. In good snow this is step-kicking; bare it is class 4 slab. In snow this is where the route's steepest ground is — the notch on the old standard south ridge line is reported at 65 degrees, which is precisely why skiers pushed a variation onto the southwest face. Above it the crest broadens into an almost level, wide-open ridge to the summit, one of the great walkable viewpoints in the range and simultaneously the top of the largest cornices most people will ever stand near. In summer that broad snow crest may instead be a scramble among rocks with steep drops on both sides.

There is also a variation that its climber did not rate: from the saddle, drop east into the basin under the east side of the south ridge, traverse up and north as far as possible, then turn west and climb beside the cliff edge. The turn involves a ten-foot step that looked trivial and was not — iced-in cracks and wrong-feeling holds, passed with ice-axe belays. The direct ridge, descended on the return, offered every ledge needed to get down. Take the ridge.

waypoints.name: Gorge Creek bridge / Gorge Creek Falls parking, SR 20 (~MP 122)
waypoints.directions: Drive SR 20 to the bridge over Gorge Creek, about 2.6 miles east of Newhalem and about the same distance west of the Gorge Lake causeway and the Diablo turnoff. Watch the sharp curve at the east end of the bridge. Park in the lot at the west end; the east lot is signed for motorhomes and oversize vehicles. There is no trail: the route leaves the highway directly.

waypoints.name: Davis Peak summit
waypoints.directions: From the east end of the bridge, cross the highway and head straight uphill into the woods. Climb the brushy lower gully and steep, trackless timber, where cliff bands near 2,400 and 2,800 ft must be turned, to granite slabs at about 4,850 ft. Scramble the Class 2-3 South Buttress, passing Point 5872 on its north side, to the 5,720 ft saddle, climb about 200 ft of slab to the sharp ridge, then follow the broad ridge to the summit.

road.name: SR 20 (North Cascades Highway)
road.status: Paved and open year-round to Newhalem, Gorge Creek and Diablo. The Gorge Creek bridge parking is plowed as part of the highway.
road.driveNote: Drive SR 20 to the bridge over Gorge Creek, about 2.6 miles east of the Seattle City Light company town of Newhalem near milepost 122, or the same distance west of the Gorge Lake causeway and the Diablo turnoff. Watch the sharp turn at the east end of the bridge — the deck is open steel grating and rings under the tyres. Parking lots sit at both ends; the east lot is for motorhomes and overlength vehicles, so use the west lot. Elevation 1,096 ft, with accessible restrooms and a short interpretive trail to the falls and the Gorge Lake overlook.
road.seasonalGate: WSDOT closes SR 20 for the winter between milepost 134 (Ross Dam Trailhead) and milepost 171 (Silver Star gate), moving down to milepost 120 (Newhalem) and milepost 178 (Early Winters) in deep winter. The Gorge Creek bridge at about milepost 122 is west of the usual gate and normally reachable all year, but a deep-winter Newhalem gate would close it — and in 2026 storm damage kept SR 20 shut between milepost 130 and milepost 156 well past the usual reopening.
